issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, 'Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident' appears trauma-incongruent unless there is a clear secondary road-traffic component; nothing elsewhere in the profile supports a vehicle-related trauma theme, so this trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the assault-focused profile.

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: The threat profile is largely centered on interpersonal/ambient danger after assault (silence, unexpected sounds), but 'Avoid Unfamiliar Places' suggests a broader environmental danger pattern. This is not inherently implausible, but combined with the car-crash trigger it contributes to a mismatched threat context that is not otherwise represented in memory or appraisals.

vignette:
Mei Lin was 51 when she first came for help, a married physician who had built her life around competence, composure, and the assumption that she could keep other people safe. She had grown up in Southeast Asia and had spent much of her adult life in the United States, where her work as a doctor demanded that she move quickly between rooms, answer interruptions without hesitation, and remain steady in front of patients and staff. After the assault, that familiar steadiness began to feel fragile to her, almost borrowed.

The assault happened in a setting that had once felt routine and predictable. Mei Lin recalled being confronted by a man she knew, and what stayed with her most were not only his face and voice but the specific physical details of the attack: the sight of his body parts close to hers in a way that felt invasive and humiliating, and the suddenness with which the situation turned from alarming to terrifying. When police became involved, their presence also lodged itself in her mind as part of the event; even later, seeing police uniforms or sensing the authority of law enforcement would bring the whole scene back with a jolt. In the days after, she found herself replaying not just what he had done, but the way he had looked to her in the moments before and during the assault, so that simply seeing him again, or anything that reminded her of him, could make her stomach tighten and her body go rigid.

As weeks passed, Mei Lin noticed that the memory did not stay in the past in any ordinary way. When it came to mind, it did not feel like an account she was telling herself from a safe distance. The terror returned with it, sharp and immediate, as if her body had not been told that the event was over. She described that the memory was so extreme it sometimes felt unreal to her, almost impossible to believe had happened to her at all. At other times, the memory arrived with a smell attached to it, an odor she could not quite place but recognized from the event itself, and that sensory fragment was enough to pull her back into the same fear she had felt then. She would catch herself freezing over a remembered detail and thinking, with a kind of stunned disbelief, that no one should have to carry something so violent inside them.

Her sense of safety in ordinary life became narrowed in ways that others around her did not always notice. Unusual silence unsettled her; when a hallway, waiting room, or her own home suddenly went quiet, she became certain that something dangerous was about to happen. Loud or unexpected sounds made her instantly alert, her attention snapping toward the source before she could settle again. Even in ordinary public settings, a stranger walking toward her could make her feel threatened, as if approach itself were a signal of danger rather than a neutral social act. These reactions showed up at work as well. In the hospital, where sudden alarms, slammed doors, or unanticipated footsteps were part of daily life, she would tense before she could explain to herself why, scanning the corridor and listening for what might come next.

Mei Lin's daily routines gradually became organized around not drawing attention to herself and not encountering reminders of the man who harmed her. She began wearing concealing clothing, choosing looser, less noticeable layers that covered her body more fully when she was out. She also worked hard to avoid anything that reminded her of the perpetrator, including places, conversations, or people who seemed to resemble him in some small way. Even with these efforts, reminders found their way in. She had started gambling to distract herself or feel excitement, describing it less as pleasure than as a way to leave her own thoughts for a while and to experience a surge of feeling that was different from dread. Yet afterward, the shame of spending money in that way sat beside the rest of what she was carrying, and it did not restore the ease she had hoped for.

Over time, Mei Lin came to feel that the assault had altered something fundamental about her understanding of the world. She said her beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed, and that she no longer had the faith in people, life, or a higher power that she once assumed would guide her through difficult times. When she thought about what had happened, she believed she would not be able to handle it, so she tried to turn away from the subject whenever possible. But the effort required to keep it away only made it loom larger in her mind, and her marriage and work life both became shaped by how carefully she managed her exposure to reminders, noise, strangers, and anything that might unexpectedly resemble the offender.

By the time she sought help, Mei Lin was no longer able to pretend that these changes were temporary. She had started to worry about how much of her life had become arranged around fear and avoidance, and she was increasingly alarmed by how often the memory, the smells, the silence, or the sight of a police presence could pull her back into the same terror. What brought her in was not a single crisis but the exhaustion of living in a world that no longer felt reliable. What she most wanted was to believe that she could think about the assault without being overwhelmed, and what she feared most was that she might never again feel safe enough to move through her life as herself.
